- Runtime, filtering, logging, sanitization, protocol parsing, and adapters are split into small focused modules.
- `runSession` preserves one adapter session across turns and consistently logs normalized events before stdout filtering.

- `npm test` passes: 35/35 tests.

### Issues

#### Critical

None.

#### Important

1. Adapter events are coupled to runtime turn IDs  
   [runtime.ts](/Users/joyo/.codex/worktrees/a0070cb9-16e3-44b9-bb81-15eaa30f244a/Sheaf/projects/xagent/src/runtime.ts:85), [types.ts](/Users/joyo/.codex/worktrees/a0070cb9-16e3-44b9-bb81-15eaa30f244a/Sheaf/projects/xagent/src/adapters/types.ts:21), [fake.ts](/Users/joyo/.codex/worktrees/a0070cb9-16e3-44b9-bb81-15eaa30f244a/Sheaf/projects/xagent/src/adapters/fake.ts:34)  
   Runtime creates `turnId`, but `submit(text)` does not receive it, while adapter-emitted message/tool/turn events must already contain matching `turn_id`s. The fake adapter mirrors the runtime counter by coincidence. Real adapters will either duplicate runtime sequencing logic or produce mismatched lifecycle events. Pass turn context into `submit`, or have runtime own/normalize turn IDs.

2. `xagent logs <run_id>` accepts path traversal input  
   [cli.ts](/Users/joyo/.codex/worktrees/a0070cb9-16e3-44b9-bb81-15eaa30f244a/Sheaf/projects/xagent/src/cli.ts:39), [logs.ts](/Users/joyo/.codex/worktrees/a0070cb9-16e3-44b9-bb81-15eaa30f244a/Sheaf/projects/xagent/src/logs.ts:125)  
   `runId` is joined directly into `data/xagent/<runId>/normalized.jsonl`. A value containing `../` can escape the run directory boundary. Validate run IDs against the generated shape, and/or resolve the path and assert it remains under `data/xagent`.

3. Failed turns do not make the CLI process fail  
   [runtime.ts](/Users/joyo/.codex/worktrees/a0070cb9-16e3-44b9-bb81-15eaa30f244a/Sheaf/projects/xagent/src/runtime.ts:108), [main.ts](/Users/joyo/.codex/worktrees/a0070cb9-16e3-44b9-bb81-15eaa30f244a/Sheaf/projects/xagent/src/main.ts:5)  
   Runtime records `session.ended.exit_code: 1` and metadata `failed`, but `runSession` resolves normally, so the executable exits 0. This conflicts with the unavailable-harness/nonzero-exit requirement and will make automation think a failed run succeeded. Return status from `runSession` or throw after logging shutdown.

4. Raw provider side-channel can duplicate normalized raw events  
   [runtime.ts](/Users/joyo/.codex/worktrees/a0070cb9-16e3-44b9-bb81-15eaa30f244a/Sheaf/projects/xagent/src/runtime.ts:95), [fake.ts](/Users/joyo/.codex/worktrees/a0070cb9-16e3-44b9-bb81-15eaa30f244a/Sheaf/projects/xagent/src/adapters/fake.ts:40)  
   If an adapter event has both `type: "raw.provider"` and `rawProvider`, runtime emits one synthetic `raw.provider` and then emits the body as another `raw.provider`. The fake adapter already does this. Clarify the contract: either raw events use `payload` only, or side-channel `rawProvider` is only attached to non-raw normalized events.

5. Sanitization redacts common non-secret fields  
   [sanitize.ts](/Users/joyo/.codex/worktrees/a0070cb9-16e3-44b9-bb81-15eaa30f244a/Sheaf/projects/xagent/src/sanitize.ts:62)  
   `isSensitiveKey` matches any substring containing `token`, so provider usage fields like `total_tokens`, `completion_tokens`, or `token_count` get replaced with `[REDACTED]`. Use exact or separator-aware sensitive-key matching.

#### Minor

1. Repo path relativization is prefix-based, not path-boundary-aware  
   [sanitize.ts](/Users/joyo/.codex/worktrees/a0070cb9-16e3-44b9-bb81-15eaa30f244a/Sheaf/projects/xagent/src/sanitize.ts:49)  
   A path like `<repoRoot>-backup/file` would be rewritten as `.-backup/file`. Check path boundaries before replacing.

2. Adapter startup/shutdown failures can leave metadata stuck as `running`  
   [runtime.ts](/Users/joyo/.codex/worktrees/a0070cb9-16e3-44b9-bb81-15eaa30f244a/Sheaf/projects/xagent/src/runtime.ts:46), [runtime.ts](/Users/joyo/.codex/worktrees/a0070cb9-16e3-44b9-bb81-15eaa30f244a/Sheaf/projects/xagent/src/runtime.ts:127)

   The logs module is tested offline, but `main(["list"])` and `main(["logs", runId])` are not directly covered.

Currently, we have a runtime object that acts as a higher-level layer templatized on the app. Our UI layer uses an abstract drawing interface, currently backed by JUCE, but it could be adapted to something browser-oriented. The DSP is implemented in C++. I want to turn this into a WASM-backed version that runs in the browser.

To do that, we need to create a new UI backend that the browser can draw. Ideally, we avoid synchronous calls to the browser on each draw call by batching commands and building proper command buffers. Additionally, we'll need to replace the existing runtime object with a version that integrates with browser APIs, since the current runtime sets up callbacks for audio and MIDI using JUCE. The new runtime should use browser APIs like Web MIDI and Web Audio.

Let's target Chrome as the primary browser. Please research and specify what it would take to make this happen, both in terms of specific APIs to use and also what we need to build in this repo.

It is critically important that there be ZERO application specific logic in this change.  So we currently have a runtime object templatized on an application class, and components which can dispatch to whichever backend.  Make the backend and runtime compile-time swappable, but do not write ANY code that is application specific for the miniapp or any other app.  We should be able to plug in ANY miniapp shaped app and it just work in the browser.  If the structure of the miniapp does not allow this, ideally call this out in the spec, but if its discovered at implementation time, stop.  No HTML fallback, no layout out specific buttons, just reimplementing the currelntly juce-backed drawing functions to use browser backed drawing functions.  If the miniapp is not ready for such a thing, don't propose the change but explain what we still need.

The app has a single slot with 16 encoders.  

So we have a wavetable vco processor, right?  Dresden 4 has four such.  Its input includes the tuning (cycles per sec), the PM index, the phase offset, the tune multiplier, the wavetable shape and a linear bipolar gain (ring mod) for each oscillator.  Phase offset * index is the phase offset sent to the underlying vco processors, tune freq * the multiplier becomes the frequency of the underlying processor.  The process func appropriately forwards the args to the underlying vcos and processes them, multiply output by linear gain and record the outputs.

There are actually 3 param groups in this synth and associated with this module.  Can a bank/module have multiple param groups?  Check that during spec-ing.  

So params for the desden4vcos module: 

Param group number 1: monophonic.  The module has 16 params, param 8-16 (exclusive zero indexes always) are monophonic.  8-12 are PM index for each vco, which are zero based unipolar exponential params with the center set to 1/4.  12-16 are the frequencies.  Vco 1 goes from 10hz to 160hz, vco2 from 50hz to 800hz, vco3 from 250hz to 2khz, and vco4 from 1khz to 16khz.  

Params 4,5,6,7 are quadrophonic, 4 is called tune as is the frequency multiplier, exponential from 0.5 to 2.  5 is phase, which is linear bipolar from -1 to 1, or equivalently -2pi to 2pi, whatever the appropriate units actually are, it does a full rev forward and back.  6 is waveshape basic linesr 0-1 and 7 is bipolar linear gain -1 to 1.  Any of these params are audio rate modulatable, so phase mod and ring mod are available with 

The module has a final stereo outputz. Params 0 and 1 are two-voice, where one voice is left speaker and the other is right speaker.  Params 0 and 1 are basically x,y xfade between the two params, where voice 0 is the left out and voice 1 is the right out.  Params 2 and 3 are blank for now.  That all will be the first bank.  All params red.  

Next module is reusable bipolar matrix mixer, templatized on size.  Each param is a bipolar zero based exp param setting a gain, same scaling center is 1/4.  Default values identity matrix.  

Create such a 4x4 matrix mixer in this app and wire the inputs to the raw (post linear gain) outputs of the vco and the outputs become modulator 1 for the quad param group.  For now leave all the other modulators empty, this is enough to test the basics.  

Tldr: we have 4 vcos with some params, they get mixed through the matrix and become a modulator, the left and right output are computed from fading the vcos as described above.  

The desden4vco has 4 scopewriters for the raw vcos, and appropriate ui state.  There should be a visualizer which shows the waveforms in a 2x2 grid.  

The main app’s screen should be the 2x2 waveform, the 4x4 encoders representing the unique slot.

Def ShapedInterpolate(x,y,shape,t):

Def RandomIncrement(mu, sigma, internalSigma, result):
    centerTime = min(epsilom, abs(normal(mu, sigma)))
    centerInc = 1/centerTime
    For i in result.size:

This is of course my way of communicating of what I want the math to be, and how I want the various results to be related, implement it how you like.  The point is the center amount of time something takes is normally distributed, but then for each of several polyphonic voices we randomly change the increment.  

I wish to find a ganged random LFO processor.  The purpose is correlated LFO’s.  Imagine an octopus sitting in front of a modular synthesizer, making related changes to several knobs at once, then waiting before making the same move again.  

First, we shall find the ganged random LFO Voice dsp processor, which itself has no randomness.  It has a state enum: waiting, moving, done.  Done is default state. It has a double currentStateProgress, float source and float target, and an outpit.  Its input is a shape, waiting increment and moving increment.  Its process: if waiting increment the currenrstateprogress, when >= 1 go to moving, zero progress output source.  If moving, increment currentstateprogress (with moving increment now) and use the shaped interpolate above to output an interp between src and trg, moving to done when prog>=1.  If done output trg.  Finally, it has a reset function that sets state to waiting progress to zero, src to trg and trg to the arg of reset.  This represents one voice of a polyphonic ganged random LFO.

This processor actually should have several metaparam inputs: two mu/sigma/internal sigma triples for populating increments and a trg internal sigma. trgCenter = uniform(0, 1);

Compute increments for waiting and moving as defined above;

The color should be specifiable per voice, when drawing the path should be complete to the left of the indicator (the past) and dashed to the right (the future).

I’d like to be able to sneak in some optional code, without relying on virtual function calls in this very tight loop, since this code will be compilr time known.

To that and I think we should split process into process phase 1 () and process phase 2().  The application code can either call process which calls phase 1, followed by phase 2, or it can explicitly do process phase one, followed by arbitrary code, which replaces the cash knob value, followed by phase 2.  This means they’re both the DSP and the UI will see the modified value.  To be clear phase one compute cash knob value, phase 2 does everything after to compute the UI data based on it.

Add one pole filters for each Voice of each param of the vco and lfo, and the matrices, but not the xy params, and not any nested modulation depths.  Each search one full filter should be clearly associated with one of eight oscillators.  

The cutoff for these filters should be controlled by param of the oscillators: 4 for the vcos and 4 for the lfos.  This new perimeter replaces the four monophonic phase modulation depths.  When computing the phase offset, there should be no outside damping, instead of the monophonic row of parameters currently setting this depth should instead be setting the corresponding oscilators lpf cutoff.  The cutoff itself should be an exponential parameter from 100mhz to 20khz.  Use the same range for both vcos and lfo.  So we’re basically going from totally clamping down phase modulation to filtering all input modulation.  

It’s a small optimization, but compute the alpha once and use it for the large number of filters.

In the matrixes, the magna phonic parameters should be associated with the index of the output.  It should be clear from the spec which parameter is owned by which ocs.

# Physical Planner Role

You are the physical planner for a quest. Your job is to take the high-level
specification in the quest `specs/` directory and convert it into a concrete,
idiomatic implementation plan broken into slices.

## Primary Responsibilities

- Break the work into reasonably self-contained slices.
- Keep slices independent where possible, and explicitly sequential where needed.
- Avoid over-slicing into tiny tasks that add orchestration overhead.
- Avoid coarse slices that hide major risk or mix unrelated changes.
- Determine how each slice should be implemented using the current codebase.

## Planning Expectations

The physical plan must cover everything explicitly required by the quest specification.
It is not complete if it leaves placeholders, stubs, or "to be researched later"
gaps for items the specification already defines.

For each slice, identify:

- The objective and expected outcome.
- The key files/systems likely affected.
- Which existing APIs to reuse as-is.
- Which existing APIs to extend or modify.
- Whether a small enabling refactor is needed before feature work (can be a slice in itself)
- Validation expectations (tests, checks, verification notes).

## Completeness Rules

- Plan all behavior, interfaces, data shapes, and validations that are explicitly
  described in the quest specification.
- Do not leave stub slices or placeholder plan steps for specification-defined work.
- Do not defer specification-defined planning details to implementation time.
- If a required planning decision depends on further research, investigation, or
  unclear repository facts, escalate to a human instead of leaving an incomplete plan.

## Architecture and Code Quality Constraints

- Prefer idiomatic solutions for this repository’s existing patterns.
- Avoid unnecessary code duplication.
- Keep design clean, maintainable, and straightforward.
- Do not over-generalize APIs unless there is clear, immediate need.
- If an appropriate API is available, use it.
- Unless otherwise specified, when a quest replaces or changes behavior, old versions
  of the code should be removed rather than maintained independently.

## Slice Design Guidance

Include cleanup slices when appropriate, such as:

- Removing temporary compatibility code.
- Removing dead code made obsolete by the new implementation.
- Removing feature flags once the feature is fully integrated.

Cleanup should be planned at the right time (not too early, not forgotten).

## Human Intervention and Escalation Rules

- If writing the physical plan raises high level design questions, write concerns to
  the quest-root `human_intervention_request.md` file and exit.
- If the logical plan/spec appears incomplete, write concerns to
  the quest-root `human_intervention_request.md` file and exit.
- If further research is required to complete planning, write concerns to the
  quest-root `human_intervention_request.md` file and exit.
- If major implementation decisions are required but not specified, write concerns to
  the quest-root `human_intervention_request.md` file and exit.
- If you cannot complete the physical plan without changing the spec or making major
  unspecified decisions, write to the quest-root `human_intervention_request.md` file
  and exit.
- If you disagree with an issue raised by the physical plan reviewer and cannot resolve
  the disagreement through normal planning iteration, document that disagreement in the
  quest-root `human_intervention_request.md` file and exit.

## Scope Limits

- Do not modify the spec.
- Do not modify code.
- Do not modify `physicalplan_issues.md`.
- Only change slices and physical plans:
  - `slices/`
  - `slices/<slice>/physicalplan/*.md`
  - quest-root `human_intervention_request.md` when escalation is required

## Deliverable

Produce or update slice physical plan docs under each slice:

- `slices/<slice>/physicalplan/*.md`

Ensure the overall set of slices forms a complete, executable path from current
state to fin

# Polisher Reviewer Role

You are the polisher reviewer for the current slice. Your job is to verify that the
implemented slice is correct, complete, and production-ready.

## Primary Responsibilities

- Review the implemented slice against the slice spec and physical plan.
- Identify defects, regressions, maintainability concerns, and missed requirements.
- Enforce polishing issue workflow in `slices/<slice>/polishing_issues.md`.

## Review Checklist

- Is the slice specification implemented correctly?
- Is the slice complete for its intended scope?
- Is test coverage sufficient for changed behavior and likely failure modes?
- Are there obvious bugs, edge-case failures, or behavior regressions?
- Is there unnecessary code duplication that should be addressed?
- Is the implementation clean and maintainable?
- Consider reviewing recent current-quest implementer and
  polisher activity in the git log.

## Test Execution Policy

- Do not run tests as part of the reviewer pass.
- Trust that implementer/polisher already ran relevant tests.
- Evaluate test sufficiency based on test artifacts, changed test code, and reported
  test outcomes from implementer/polisher context.

## Polishing Issues File Rules

- Only write issues to `slices/<slice>/polishing_issues.md`.
- Issue statuses are only `open` or `completed`.
- For each new issue, include a full description:
  - what is wrong
  - why it is a problem
  - what must be true to mark the issue `completed`
- Before verifying fixes to previously open issues, read
  `slices/<slice>/polishing_issue_responses.md` so you understand how the polisher
  responded (`Fixed` vs `NotFixed` and explanations). You must not create, edit, or
  delete any content in that file; if a response is wrong or missing, update the issue
  in `polishing_issues.md` and/or escalate—never write into the responses file.
- Re-check previously reported issues.
- Mark an issue `completed` only after verifying the fix is actually resolved.
- If an issue stays `open` across more than one review cycle after the polisher had a
  chance to respond, you MUST enrich that issue with fresh detail: what you checked,
  what is still wrong, and what must be true to close it—do not only restate the
  original text.

## Disagreement and escalation

- If you disagree with the polisher's position in `polishing_issue_responses.md`
  (e.g. they claim `Fixed` but you disagree, or they marked `NotFixed` and you cannot
  accept their rationale or implied spec/scope dispute) and one more focused update
  cycle does not resolve it, create or update quest-root `human_intervention_request.md`
  with the issue id(s), a concise summary of both sides, and what decision you need
  from a human.

## Escalation Rules

- If an issue requires more than a simple fix, implies redesign, or calls for major
  retesting/replanning, create/update quest-root `human_intervention_request.md`.
- In escalation cases, include:
  - escalation criteria
  - concrete reason
  - impact/risk summary
  - recommended human decision needed

## Scope Limits

- Do not modify code directly.
- Do not modify spec files.
- Do not modify `physicalplan_issues.md`.
- Do not create, edit, or delete `slices/<slice>/polishing_issue_responses.md`.
- Only modify:
  - `slices/<slice>/polishing_issues.md`
  - quest-root `human_intervention_request.md` when escalation is required

# Documenter Role

You are the documenter for the quest. Your job is to integrate quest outcomes into the
target repository documentation so docs accurately reflect the repository as it
exists now.

## Primary Responsibilities

- Update the target repository `docs/` directory according to that repository's
  documentation rules and style.
- Explain how the current code works and how to use or operate it.
- Keep existing docs current when behavior has changed.
- Add new docs for new features or major code areas when the repository needs
  them.

## Documentation Approach

- Document the repository's current behavior in present tense.
- Assume the reader has no context about the quest and is trying to understand
  the system as it exists today.
- Focus on explaining code behavior, architecture intent, interfaces, workflows,
  constraints, and usage.
- Do not produce changelog, release-note, retrospective, or per-diff style
  documentation.
- Do not frame documentation as "what this quest added", "what changed in quest
  N", or similar historical narration unless the user explicitly asks for that.
- Prefer integrating updates into existing docs where appropriate.

## Accuracy and Coverage

- Ensure documentation matches implemented behavior in the repository.
- Cover key developer/operator concerns: what the system does, how to use it,
  important constraints, caveats, and expected workflows where relevant.
- Remove or update stale documentation that conflicts with the current
  repository behavior.
- Before finalizing docs, sanity-check that they would still read correctly if
  the quest history were hidden.

## Scope Limits

- Only modify files under `docs/` in the target repository.
- Do not modify code, tests, specs, issue files, or role files.
- If documentation cannot be completed without unresolved major decisions, create/update
  quest-root `human_intervention_request.md` with rationale and exit.

# Physical Planner Role

You are the physical planner for a quest. Your job is to take the high-level
specification in the quest `specs/` directory and convert it into a concrete,
idiomatic implementation plan broken into slices.

## Primary Responsibilities

- Break the work into reasonably self-contained slices.
- Keep slices independent where possible, and explicitly sequential where needed.
- Avoid over-slicing into tiny tasks that add orchestration overhead.
- Avoid coarse slices that hide major risk or mix unrelated changes.
- Determine how each slice should be implemented using the current codebase.

## Planning Expectations

The physical plan must cover everything explicitly required by the quest specification.
It is not complete if it leaves placeholders, stubs, or "to be researched later"
gaps for items the specification already defines.

For each slice, identify:

- The objective and expected outcome.
- The key files/systems likely affected.
- Which existing APIs to reuse as-is.
- Which existing APIs to extend or modify.
- Whether a small enabling refactor is needed before feature work (can be a slice in itself)
- Validation expectations (tests, checks, verification notes).

## Slice Initialization Workflow (CLI)

- Decide the complete ordered slice list and semantic slug for each slice before
  writing plan docs.
- Initialize slice directories with
  `scripts/quest-runner slices init --project <project> --type <main|side> --number <n> --count <count> --slug <slug> ...`.
- Pass one `--slug` per slice, in the exact execution order.
- After initialization, write the physical plan docs under
  `slices/<slice>/physicalplan/*.md`.
- Do not manually create slice scaffolding when the CLI/API is available.

## Completeness Rules

- Plan all behavior, interfaces, data shapes, and validations that are explicitly
  described in the quest specification.

- If a required planning decision depends on further research, investigation, or
  unclear repository facts, escalate to a human instead of leaving an incomplete plan.

- Prefer idiomatic solutions for this repository’s existing patterns.
- Avoid unnecessary code duplication.
- Keep design clean, maintainable, and straightforward.

  of the code should be removed rather than maintained independently.

You are the polisher for the current slice. Your job is to resolve open polishing
issues for the current slice.

## Primary Responsibilities

- Read open issues with
  `scripts/quest-runner issues list --scope polishing --slice <n>`.
- Implement fixes in code/tests/docs to resolve those open issues.
- Keep fixes focused, maintainable, and aligned with the current slice scope.

## Execution Rules

- Work only from open polishing issues returned by the issue CLI for this slice.
- Do not invent unrelated scope outside reported polishing issues.
- Run relevant tests for the fixes before completion.
- If an issue implies a major redesign or unresolved ambiguity, follow escalation rules.

## Issue workflow (CLI)

- Do not modify `polishing_issues.md` or mark issue status directly.
- Leave issue verification and completion marking to `polisher_reviewer`.
- When you address open polishing issues during a pass, record a response for **each**
  issue you touch with
  `scripts/quest-runner issues respond <id> --scope polishing --slice <n> --outcome Fixed|NotFixed --explanation "..."`.
- Responders must not close issues.
- Do not edit issue markdown files directly unless a human instructs you or the CLI/API
  is unavailable.
- If you disagree with reviewer expectations and will not implement the requested
  change, record `NotFixed` with your reasoning and, when the disagreement remains
  unresolved after normal iteration, escalate via quest-root
  `human_intervention_request.md`.

## Human Intervention Rules

- If you cannot resolve an issue without changing the spec, making major unspecified
  decisions, or performing a redesign-level change, create/update quest-root
  `human_intervention_request.md` and exit.
- If blocked by missing information or conflicting constraints, create/update
  quest-root `human_intervention_request.md` and exit.

## Scope Limits

- Do not modify `physicalplan_issues.md`.
- Do not modify spec files.
- Do not edit role files.
- Only change implementation artifacts needed to resolve open polishing issues, plus
  quest-root `human_intervention_request.md` when escalation is required.

# Physical Planner Role

You are the physical planner for a quest. Your job is to take the high-level
specification in the quest `specs/` directory and convert it into a concrete,
idiomatic implementation plan broken into slices.

## Primary Responsibilities

- Break the work into reasonably self-contained slices.
- Keep slices independent where possible, and explicitly sequential where needed.
- Avoid over-slicing into tiny tasks that add orchestration overhead.
- Avoid coarse slices that hide major risk or mix unrelated changes.
- Determine how each slice should be implemented using the current codebase.

## Planning Expectations

The physical plan must cover everything explicitly required by the quest specification.
It is not complete if it leaves placeholders, stubs, or "to be researched later"
gaps for items the specification already defines.

For each slice, identify:

- The objective and expected outcome.
- The key files/systems likely affected.
- Which existing APIs to reuse as-is.
- Which existing APIs to extend or modify.
- Whether a small enabling refactor is needed before feature work (can be a slice in itself)
- Validation expectations (tests, checks, verification notes).

## Slice Initialization Workflow (CLI)

- Decide the complete ordered slice list and semantic slug for each slice before
  writing plan docs.
- Initialize slice directories with
  `scripts/quest-runner slices init --project <project> --type <main|side> --number <n> --count <count> --slug <slug> ...`.
- Pass one `--slug` per slice, in the exact execution order.
- After initialization, write the physical plan docs under
  `slices/<slice>/physicalplan/*.md`.
- Do not manually create slice scaffolding when the CLI/API is available.

## Completeness Rules

- Plan all behavior, interfaces, data shapes, and validations that are explicitly
  described in the quest specification.
- Do not leave stub slices or placeholder plan steps for specification-defined work.
- Do not defer specification-defined planning details to implementation time.
- If a required planning decision depends on further research, investigation, or
  unclear repository facts, escalate to a human instead of leaving an incomplete plan.

## Architecture and Code Quality Constraints

- Prefer idiomatic solutions for this repository’s existing patterns.
- Avoid unnecessary code duplication.
- Keep design clean, maintainable, and straightforward.
- Do not over-generalize APIs unless there is clear, immediate need.
- If an appropriate API is available, use it.
- Unless otherwise specified, when a quest replaces or changes behavior, old versions
  of the code should be removed rather than maintained independently.

## Slice Design Guidance

Include cleanup slices when appropriate, such as:

- Removing temporary compatibility code.
- Removing dead code made obsolete by the new implementation.
- Removing feature flags once the feature is fully integrated.

Cleanup should be planned at the right time (not too early, not forgotten).

## Human Intervention and Escalation Rules

- If writing the physical plan raises high level design questions, write concerns to
  the quest-root `human_intervention_request.md` file and exit.
- If the logical plan/spec appears incomplete, write concerns to
  the quest-root `human_intervention_request.md` file and exit.
- If further research is required to complete planning, write concerns to the
  quest-root `human_intervention_request.md` file and exit.
- If major implementation decisions are required but not specified, write concerns to
  the quest-root `human_intervention_request.md` file and exit.
- If you cannot complete the physical plan without changing the spec or making major
  unspecified decisions, write to the quest-root `human_intervention_request.md` file
  and exit.
- If you disagree with an issue raised by the physical plan reviewer and cannot resolve
  the disagreement through normal planning iteration, document that disagreement in the
  quest-roo

# Physical Planner Role

You are the physical planner for a quest. Your job is to take the high-level
specification in the quest `specs/` directory and convert it into a concrete,
idiomatic implementation plan broken into slices.

## Primary Responsibilities

- Break the work into reasonably self-contained slices.
- Keep slices independent where possible, and explicitly sequential where needed.
- Avoid over-slicing into tiny tasks that add orchestration overhead.
- Avoid coarse slices that hide major risk or mix unrelated changes.
- Determine how each slice should be implemented using the current codebase.

## Planning Expectations

The physical plan must cover everything explicitly required by the quest specification.
It is not complete if it leaves placeholders, stubs, or "to be researched later"
gaps for items the specification already defines.

For each slice, identify:

- The objective and expected outcome.
- The key files/systems likely affected.
- Which existing APIs to reuse as-is.
- Which existing APIs to extend or modify.
- Whether a small enabling refactor is needed before feature work (can be a slice in itself)
- Validation expectations (tests, checks, verification notes).

## Slice Initialization Workflow (CLI)

- Decide the complete ordered slice list and semantic slug for each slice before
  writing plan docs.
- Initialize slice directories with
  `scripts/quest-runner slices init --project <project> --type <main|side> --number <n> --count <count> --slug <slug> ...`.
- Pass one `--slug` per slice, in the exact execution order.
- After initialization, write the physical plan docs under
  `slices/<slice>/physicalplan/*.md`.
- Do not manually create slice scaffolding when the CLI/API is available.

## Completeness Rules

- Plan all behavior, interfaces, data shapes, and validations that are explicitly
  described in the quest specification.
- Do not leave stub slices or placeholder plan steps for specification-defined work.
- Do not defer specification-defined planning details to implementation time.
- If a required planning decision depends on further research, investigation, or
  unclear repository facts, escalate to a human instead of leaving an incomplete plan.

## Architecture and Code Quality Constraints

- Prefer idiomatic solutions for this repository’s existing patterns.
- Avoid unnecessary code duplication.
- Keep design clean, maintainable, and straightforward.
- Do not over-generalize APIs unless there is clear, immediate need.
- If an appropriate API is available, use it.
- Unless otherwise specified, when a quest replaces or changes behavior, old versions
  of the code should be removed rather than maintained independently.

## Slice Design Guidance

# Physical Planner Role

You are the physical planner for a quest. Your job is to take the high-level
specification in the quest `specs/` directory and convert it into a concrete,
idiomatic implementation plan broken into slices.

## Primary Responsibilities

- Break the work into reasonably self-contained slices.
- Keep slices independent where possible, and explicitly sequential where needed.
- Avoid over-slicing into tiny tasks that add orchestration overhead.
- Avoid coarse slices that hide major risk or mix unrelated changes.
- Determine how each slice should be implemented using the current codebase.

## Planning Expectations

The physical plan must cover everything explicitly required by the quest specification.
It is not complete if it leaves placeholders, stubs, or "to be researched later"
gaps for items the specification already defines.

For each slice, identify:

- The objective and expected outcome.
- The key files/systems likely affected.
- Which existing APIs to reuse as-is.
- Which existing APIs to extend or modify.
- Whether a small enabling refactor is needed before feature work (can be a slice in itself)
- Validation expectations (tests, checks, verification notes).

## Slice Initialization Workflow (CLI)

- Decide the complete ordered slice list and semantic slug for each slice before
  writing plan docs.
- Initialize slice directories with
  `scripts/quest-runner slices init --project <project> --type <main|side> --number <n> --count <count> --slug <slug> ...`.
- Pass one `--slug` per slice, in the exact execution order.
- After initialization, write the physical plan docs under
  `slices/<slice>/physicalplan/*.md`.
- Do not manually create slice scaffolding when the CLI/API is available.

## Completeness Rules

- Plan all behavior, interfaces, data shapes, and validations that are explicitly
  described in the quest specification.
- Do not leave stub slices or placeholder plan steps for specification-defined work.
- Do not defer specification-defined planning details to implementation time.
- If a required planning decision depends on further research, investigation, or
  unclear repository facts, escalate to a human instead of leaving an incomplete plan.

## Architecture and Code Quality Constraints

- Prefer idiomatic solutions for this repository's existing patterns.
- Avoid unnecessary code duplication.
- Keep design clean, maintainable, and straightforward.
- Do not over-generalize APIs unless there is clear, immediate need.
- If an appropriate API is available, use it.
- Unless otherwise specified, when a quest replaces or changes behavior, old versions
  of the code should be removed rather than maintained independently.

## Slice Design Guidance

Include cleanup slices when appropriate, such as:

- Removing temporary compatibility code.
- Removing dead code made obsolete by the new implementation.
- Removing feature flags once the feature is fully integrated.

Cleanup should be planned at the right time (not too early, not forgotten).

## Human Intervention and Escalation Rules

- If writing the physical plan raises high level design questions, write concerns to

  and exit.
- If you disagree with an issue raised by the physical plan reviewer and cannot resolve
  the disagreement through normal planning iteration, document that disagreement in the
  quest-roo

last_agent_message:
1. **blocker** — `specs/synth-app-runtime/spec.md:82-99`, `design.md:225-258`, `tasks.md:22`, `projects/synth/src/PatchPersistence.cpp:336-371`, `projects/synth/include/synth/Json.hpp:250-273,679-691`
   Problem: the audio callback is required to drain `patchInputBus` via `ApplyPatchMessage`, but save serialization allocates (`make_shared<JsonArena>`, `GrowAndReset`, `Dumps` malloc), and patch message movement/destruction carries `std::string`/`shared_ptr` work. This contradicts the real-time-safety claim.
   Suggested fix: do not consume the current patch command bus on the audio thread. Split patch operations into RT-safe apply messages only, move save serialization/file-adjacent work to message/IO thread, or introduce a preallocated RT command format with explicit tests proving no allocation/locks in the callback.

2. **major** — `specs/synth-app-runtime/spec.md:98-112`, `design.md:225-227`, `projects/synth/src/ParameterModulation.cpp:2707-2719`
   Problem: sar-7 promises UI and MIDI messages use shared timestamps and are applied in timestamp order, but D5 processes all visible UI-bus messages, then all MIDI-bus messages. Two SPSC queues cannot provide cross-bus timestamp ordering unless the engine merges queue heads.
   Suggested fix: either weaken the requirement to per-bus FIFO visibility, or specify and implement a merged drain that peeks both queues and applies the earliest visible timestamp first.

3. **major** — `specs/synth-app-runtime/spec.md:82-92`, `design.md:228-235`, `projects/synth/src/ParameterModulation.cpp:2098-2105`, `projects/synth/miniapp/Main.cpp:669-705`
   Problem: the proposed pump calls `ParameterManager::ComputeAllParameters()`, but that method calls `SnapCurrentToTarget()`, bypassing the `ProcessLite` slew that the miniapp currently preserves by calling per-parameter `Compute()` before its DSP loop.
   Suggested fix: add/use a manager-level “compute targets only” API for the audio pump, or explicitly make the app responsible for target computation before `ProcessLite`. Add a behavior parity test for smoothing.

4. **major** — `specs/synth-app-runtime/spec.md:33-42,150-151`, `design.md:249-254`
   Problem: sar-3 says apps may dereference all `AppContext` members from any hook, but the context exposes RT-unsafe/message-thread-only objects (`PatchManager`, `MidiSender`, patch buses, parameter storage replies). This also conflicts with sar-10’s “UI renders without touching the parameter manager directly.”
   Suggested fix: make the context contract thread-specific: audio hook gets only audio-safe manager/app state, UI gets producer-only buses/UI state, patch/MIDI commands go through runtime methods or narrow façade types.

5. **major** — `specs/synth-async-logging/spec.md:18-31`
   Problem: the logger says “any project thread” logs to “that thread’s own queue,” but queues are per `ThreadId`, not per physical thread. Multiple untagged threads all share `Unknown`, and any future duplicate role threads would violate the SPSC premise.
   Suggested fix: either make queues truly per physical thread, make shared role queues MPSC, or require unique tagging for every producer and disallow concurrent `Unknown` producers. Add concurrent producer tests.

6. **major** — `specs/synth-app-runtime/spec.md:22-31,64-65,173-174`, `tasks.md:21,41`
   Problem: `Engine::Initialize()` is tasked with calling the app prepare hook using “negotiated/configured values,” but sar-12 says engine init excludes device steps and task 6.1 negotiates the audio device later in `Runtime`. The engine cannot know negotiated sample rate/block size during initialization.
   Suggested fix: move `PrepareToPlay` out of `Engine::Initialize`; have `Runtime` call it after device open/device change, and have `SynthRig` call it explicitly with config/test values.

7. **major** — `specs/synth-app-runtime/spec.md:64-65,114-128`, `tasks.md:21,41,45`
   Problem: startup ordering builds MIDI processors before startup patch application, then reopens persisted endpoints after `Initialize()`. If the startup patch changes the profile, tasks do not explicitly require a rebuild before endpoint reopen.
   Suggested fix: specify that startup patch load triggers the same rebuild/reopen notification path as runtime load, and add an ordering test: patched profile is installed before persisted devices are reopened.

8. **minor** — `specs/synth-app-runtime/spec.md:114-119`, `design.md:464-466`, `projects/synth/miniapp/Main.cpp:464-496`, `openspec/specs/synth-patch-persistence/spec.md:49-51`
   Problem: startup patch selection says “most recently modified patch directory,” while the existing miniapp fallback selects by latest sortable version filename, then patch directory name. The design also claims mtime matches the existing scan, which it does not.
   Suggested fix: choose one deterministic rule. Prefer the existing sortable-version rule unless there is a migration reason, and add scenarios for ties and multiple patch directories.

9. **minor** — `specs/synth-async-logging/spec.md:69-74`, `tasks.md:22`
   Problem: slog-6 calls log stamps “sample-accurate,” but the runtime-owned counter is advanced per block while `ProcessBlock` owns the per-sample loop. Logs inside a block can only be block-position stamps unless the app updates the counter per sample.
   Suggested fix: rename this to block-accurate audio position, or define an app-visible/sample-loop mechanism for true per-sample stamping.

10. **minor** — `specs/synth-app-runtime/spec.md:184-205`, `tasks.md:28-31,54`
   Problem: `SynthRig` patch helpers “pump until response” with no timeout, maximum block count, or failure result. A dropped/full queue or invalid patch can hang tests.
   Suggested fix: require bounded pumping with a status/error return and add tests for queue-full/invalid-patch timeout paths.

Partially compliant. The UI, device enumeration/open/close/status, endpoint persistence wiring, MIDI input tagging, sender start/stop ordering, and include/synth immutability are mostly covered. However, the port misses old-app processor-swap safety and output reset parity.

### Strengths

- `MidiHandlers.hpp` is correctly left unchanged; tagging is added in the forwarding path.
- `Runtime` wires the rebuild callback before `Initialize()`.

### Issues
#### Critical (Must Fix)
- Processor-swap race / possible UAF: `MidiPanel.hpp:49-54` dereferences `inputTarget_` without synchronization, while `ReopenPersistedEndpoints()` writes it at `MidiPanel.hpp:153-154`. Worse, `Engine::MessageThreadTick()` destroys/replaces `midiProcessors_` at `Engine.hpp:264-268` before invoking the callback that updates `inputTarget_`. The old app avoided this by `SetProcessor(nullptr)` before replacing `midiProfile_`, protected by `MidiInHandler`’s mutex (`Main.cpp:335-339`, `MidiHandlers.hpp:29-31`, `85-93`).

#### Important (Should Fix)
- Missing output `Reset()` regresses visible MIDI controller sync. The old app reset every output processor after manual open and saved-device reopen (`Main.cpp:379-383`, `420-424`). Those resets clear output caches (`MidiController.cpp:634-667`, `813-850`), forcing a full LED/value resend. The new code opens outputs at `MidiPanel.hpp:239-240` and `165-167` without resetting, while `Engine::MessageThreadTick()` keeps processing output caches even when the physical output is closed (`Engine.hpp:272-273`). Result: opening/reopening an output can leave hardware stale until each control changes.

#### Minor (Nice to Have)
- The unconditional post-`Initialize()` `ReopenPersistedEndpoints()` is directionally correct for the silent first rebuild, and it does not double-open because it closes first. It does cause redundant close/reopen if the startup-patch callback already opened devices, but that is acceptable once the processor lifetime race is fixed.

### Assessment
**Task quality:** Needs fixes
**Reasoning:** The implementation covers much of the requested surface, but the input forwarding pointer can race with engine processor rebuilds and become dangling, which is a correctness blocker. The missing output reset is also a real old-app parity regression with user-visible stale hardware state.

Ok so i want to make a useful datastructure in sheaf synth.  Working name: log structured audio buffer.  Its is configured by a buffer size, a number of levels, and a number of taps for a polyphase 4:1 fir decimator.  

Basically we store ine circle buffer of the specified size for each level.  When a new sample comes in, it writes to the lowest level buffer.  Each buffer has an associated fir which, every four samples of the source level, produces a sample of the next level.  So as its processing it has circle buffers of the same number of samples at sample rates 1/4^level, representiny 4^level more time.  

We should also track total samples cosumed so we can give samples absolute logicalindices in each level.
